newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House approves balanced budget amendment.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House approves balanced budget amendment.

text.p: The U.S. House of Representatives early on Wednesday approved a five-year balanced budget agreement, after narrowly defeating an amendment that could have undermined the crucial deal.
The budget serves as the blueprint for $1.5 trillion in U.S. government spending in the coming 1998 fiscal year and sets goals for deficit reduction through 2002.
The Senate, the upper house of America's Congress which also began its budget agreement debate on Tuesday, was expected to pass it on Thursday.

The budget slows the growth of government spending for the next five years, cuts Medicare by $115 billion and brings the deficit down to zero by 2002 from this year's forecast level of $67 billion. It also provides a net $85 billion tax cut.
The House approved the budget 333-99 immediately after a cliffhanger vote of 216-214 defeated an amendment which sought to boost funds for roads and mass transit by $12 billion through the year 2002.
Anxious Republican leaders had feared until the last moment that the transportation amendment could pass and throw their budget strategy into disarray.

On final passage, a majority of President Bill Clinton's Democrats supported the budget despite the decision by Democrat Minority Leader Richard Gephardt to oppose it. Democrats voted for the budget by a margin of 132-72 and Republicans voted for it by 201-26.

The House also defeated amendments offered by the Congressional Black Caucus to cut defence spending by $190 billion over five years, a conservative Republican amendment to save more from domestic programmes and two other amendments that sought to increase social spending.

Congressional budget committees said that over its five years, the plan cut $304 billion in spending from what would have occurred without changes in policy but gave Clinton $33 billion to spend on education, the environment and other domestic priorities.
